what: Australia 'deeply frustrated' over Laos methanol poisoning charges

clean_source_blocks.text: Holly Bowles, left, and Bianca Jones were visiting Laos from Australia The Australian government has said it is "deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed" that Laos is not pursuing more serious charges in relation to the deaths of six backpackers who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol in 2024. Australians Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, were among six people who died at a hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024. The statement comes after reports in Australian media that Laos would press charges that collectively carry penalties of up to one year in jail and a fine of A$1600 ($1100; £829) against those allegedly responsible. Australian Foreign Ministry Penny Wong said it had summoned Laos' ambassador to Canberra. Laos has yet to confirm any charges but the BBC understands authorities there will hold a press conference later on Friday.
Media reports say Laos will press charges of up to one year in jail against those allegedly responsible.

Parents of a young woman who died from methanol poisoning in Laos have revealed their heartache over a lack of criminal charges relating to the deaths of their daughter and her friend. Melbourne teens Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, died after consuming drinks containing the deadly alcohol while staying at a hostel in the tourist town Vang Vieng in November 2024. Those responsible for the deaths are likely to receive a maximum penalty of one year in jail and a collective fine of $1600. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today They are not even expected to be charged with breaching hygiene laws, which would add five years to the sentence. Holly’s parents, Samantha Morton and Shaun Bowles, said they were crushed to learn of the light punishment.

Holly Bowles, left, and Bianca Jones were visiting Laos from Australia

The Australian government has said it is "deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed" that Laos is not pursuing more serious charges in relation to the deaths of six backpackers who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol in 2024.

Australians Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, were among six people who died at a hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024.

The statement comes after reports in Australian media that Laos would press charges that collectively carry penalties of up to one year in jail and a fine of A$1600 ($1100; £829) against those allegedly responsible.

Australian Foreign Ministry Penny Wong said it had summoned Laos' ambassador to Canberra.

Laos has yet to confirm any charges but the BBC understands authorities there will hold a press conference later on Friday.

"This devastating news will only add to the immense pain and grief suffered by the families and friends of Holly and Bianca," Australia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"We have consistently made clear our expectations that charges should reflect the gravity of the tragedy. This includes the Prime Minister and I expressing these expectations directly to our respective counterparts."

Jones and Bowles were among six foreign tourists who died after consuming free drinks at the Nana Backpacker Hostel in the popular backpacking town of Vang Vieng. The other victims include British, American and Danish tourists.

It is thought the free shots were tainted with methanol, a toxic substance normally found in paint thinner but that is sometimes mixed with alcohol illegally to cut costs.

Earlier this year, ten people connected to the hostel were charged with destroying evidence, receiving suspended sentences and fines of $185 (£135) each - something described by the brother of one victim as an "absolute joke".

payload.title: Australia arvostelee Laosin aikeita metanolimyrkytyksen syytteissä
payload.summary: Australia on kutsunut Laosin suurlähettilään kuultavaksi saatuaan tietoja lieviksi arvioiduista syytteistä kuuden reppumatkailijan kuolemaan johtaneessa metanolimyrkytyksessä.
payload.content:
Australian hallitus on ilmaissut syvän turhautumisensa ja pettymyksensä tietoihin, joiden mukaan Laos ei aio nostaa vakavampia syytteitä kuuden reppumatkailijan kuolemaan johtaneesta metanolimyrkytyksestä. Australialaismedian mukaan suunnitelluista syytteistä voisi seurata yhteensä enintään vuoden vankeusrangaistus ja 1 600 Australian dollarin sakko.

## Laos ei ole vielä vahvistanut syytteitä

Laosin viranomaiset eivät ole vahvistaneet syytteitä tai mahdollisia rangaistuksia. BBC:n tietojen mukaan viranomaisten on määrä järjestää asiasta tiedotustilaisuus perjantaina.

Australian ulkoministeri Penny Wong kertoi hallituksen kutsuneen Laosin Canberran-suurlähettilään kuultavaksi. Hallitus kuvaili tilannetta syvästi turhauttavaksi ja katkeraksi pettymykseksi, koska sen mielestä tiedossa olevat syytteet eivät vastaa tapahtumien vakavuutta.

Australian tiedotusvälineiden mukaan Laosin ministeriö oli ilmoittanut australialaisuhrien perheille, että vakavimmistakin suunnitelluista syytteistä voisi seurata vain sakko ja enintään vuosi vankeutta. Tiedot perustuvat toistaiseksi julkisuuteen saatuihin raportteihin, eivät Laosin viranomaisten lopulliseen vahvistukseen.

## Kuusi matkailijaa kuoli Vang Viengissä

Australialaiset Bianca Jones ja Holly Morton-Bowles, molemmat 19-vuotiaita, olivat kuuden marraskuussa 2024 kuolleen reppumatkailijan joukossa. He olivat majoittuneet hostellissa Laosin suositussa matkailukaupungissa Vang Viengissä ja nauttineet metanolia sisältäneitä juomia.

Nuorten vanhemmat ovat arvostelleet odotettavissa olevia seuraamuksia ankarasti. Biancan isä Mark Jones sanoi Australian ABC:lle raivostumisen olevan liian lievä ilmaus hänen tunteilleen. Hollyn isä Shaun Bowles puolestaan kuvaili tietoja erittäin vaikeiksi käsittää. Hollyn vanhemmat Samantha Morton ja Shaun Bowles kertoivat olevansa järkyttyneitä rangaistusten lievyydestä.

## Hostelliin liittyviä henkilöitä tuomittiin aiemmin

Aiemmin tänä vuonna kymmenen hostelliin liittynyttä henkilöä sai syytteet todisteiden hävittämisestä. Heille määrättiin ehdollisia vankeusrangaistuksia ja kullekin 185 dollarin sakko.

7NEWSin mukaan epäiltyjä ei myöskään odoteta syytettävän hygieniasäännösten rikkomisesta. Tällainen syyte voisi australialaismedian mukaan pidentää mahdollista vankeusrangaistusta viidellä vuodella. Laosin tulevan tiedotustilaisuuden odotetaan täsmentävän, mitä syytteitä tapauksessa lopulta nostetaan.

Holly Bowles, left, and Bianca Jones were visiting Laos from Australia The Australian government has said it is "deeply frustrated and bitterly disappointed" that Laos is not pursuing more serious charges in relation to the deaths of six backpackers who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol in 2024. Australians Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, were among six people who died at a hostel in Vang Vieng in November 2024. The statement comes after reports in Australian media that Laos would press charges that collectively carry penalties of up to one year in jail and a fine of A$1600 ($1100; £829) against those allegedly responsible. Australian Foreign Ministry Penny Wong said it had summoned Laos' ambassador to Canberra. Laos has yet to confirm any charges but the BBC understands authorities there will hold a press conference later on Friday.

Media reports say Laos will press charges of up to one year in jail against those allegedly responsible.

Parents of a young woman who died from methanol poisoning in Laos have revealed their heartache over a lack of criminal charges relating to the deaths of their daughter and her friend. Melbourne teens Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, both 19, died after consuming drinks containing the deadly alcohol while staying at a hostel in the tourist town Vang Vieng in November 2024. Those responsible for the deaths are likely to receive a maximum penalty of one year in jail and a collective fine of $1600. Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today They are not even expected to be charged with breaching hygiene laws, which would add five years to the sentence. Holly’s parents, Samantha Morton and Shaun Bowles, said they were crushed to learn of the light punishment.

Earlier this year, ten people connected to the hostel were charged with destroying evidence, receiving suspended sentences and fines of $185 (£135) each - something described by the brother of one victim as an "absolute joke". And on Thursday, Australian media ran reports saying that the Laos ministry had written to the families of the Australian victims with information that the most serious charges expected for those responsible carried only the possibility of a fine and a one-year prison sentence. Bianca's father, Mark Jones, told Australian broadcaster ABC that "[feeling] furious would be an understatement" while Holly's father, Shaun Bowles, said it was "very hard to comprehend" the expected charges.
